summary.text: A 3-year-old child was presented at the 15th ECHO session by a spoke site with abdominal swelling progressing over several weeks, watery stool, nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting and fevers. He appeared ill, with diffuse lymphadenopathy and a grossly distended, tender abdomen with a palpable mass, described in the discussion as rapidly enlarging. Laboratory tests revealed anemia and mildly elevated blood urea and creatinine.

The hub experts raised the possibility of Burkitt lymphoma, and further local evaluations were deferred to facilitate urgent transfer to MTRH. A rapid biopsy confirmed Burkitt lymphoma. Table 1 lists an abdominal CT under imaging, but the text does not describe it being performed.

The child died during initial prephase chemotherapy. The narrative attributes the death to tumor lysis complications, whereas Table 1 calls the tumor lysis syndrome suspected, and the discussion adds renal failure.

summary.text: A 5-year-old male was presented at the 34th ECHO session with right-sided abdominal swelling and 4 months of weight loss, night sweats and watery stools. Examination showed a large nontender abdominal mass. He was anemic, but other laboratory values were normal.

The spoke site, concerned for a malignancy, obtained an abdominal ultrasound and computed tomography scan remarkable for a 10 × 8-cm mass in the right pelvis consistent with a lymphoma. A colonoscopy with preliminary biopsy favored BL. ECHO participants reviewed the reports and agreed with the diagnosis of BL.
After the ECHO session the patient was transferred immediately to MTRH for chemotherapy, which was completed without significant complications. He survived and completed the chemotherapy regimen.

summary.text: A 12-year-old child was presented at the 40th ECHO session with 4 months of progressive, worsening bilateral knee arthralgias. He had been admitted to the county hospital twice in the preceding 4 months for anemia requiring transfusions without an identified cause. On his third presentation he was sick-appearing, pale, tachypneic and edematous, with pancytopenia without peripheral blast cells.

The spoke participant was concerned for malignancy, recognizing possible leukemia, and recognized an impending oncologic emergency, prompting emergent referral to MTRH through the hub team before the ECHO presentation. A same-day transfer followed, and he was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
After diagnosis he tolerated induction chemotherapy well but ultimately died while receiving consolidation chemotherapy because of infection; Table 1 names invasive varicella infection on treatment.
